chapters.name: Chapter 1: How LLMs work and how to instruct them

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How an LLM writes: tokens, prediction and context
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain why an LLM can sound right and still be wrong.
This lesson builds toward: Given a wrong but confident answer from a chatbot, you will explain how tokens, prediction and the context window can make an LLM sound right and still be wrong, in your own words, naming at least two causes.
An LLM writes one small piece of text at a time. These pieces are called tokens: a short word, part of a longer word or a punctuation mark. At each step the model predicts a likely next token from everything it has seen so far.
Everything the model can see at once is its context window: the system prompt, the conversation, any documents you paste and its own answer so far. Anything outside the context window does not exist for the model. It has no memory of past chats unless the app adds them.
Because it predicts likely text, an LLM can write a smooth answer that is false. It is not looking facts up unless it has a search tool. Your prompt, the context you give it and the checks you build are what make it reliable.
Words to know:
- Token: a small piece of text, often part of a word, that an LLM reads and writes.
- Context window: all the text the model can see at one time.
- Prediction: the model choosing a likely next token based on what came before.
Try it now: In a free chatbot, ask: "How many letters r are in the word strawberry? Then explain how tokens might make this hard for you." Note whether the first answer was right, and why tokens matter.
You can now explain tokens and the context window, and why an LLM needs checking.

check.q: What does an LLM do when it writes an answer?
options: Looks the answer up in a checked database
Predicts likely next tokens, one at a time
Copies a stored answer written by a person
Runs a search and reads the top result
check.why: An LLM predicts text token by token, so it can sound fluent without checking facts.

check.q: A chatbot gives a confident answer about a rule that matters to your work. What do you do?
options: Use it, because it sounded sure
Ask it the same question again until it agrees
Check the rule against a trusted source before using it
Paste the answer into a new chat to confirm it
check.why: A smooth answer can still be wrong, so important facts need a trusted source.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The parts of a strong prompt
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a prompt with a role, task, context, rules and output format.
This lesson builds toward: For one job in your agent, you will write a system prompt with a role, a task, context, rules and an output format, with every part present and rules that can be checked.
A strong prompt for an agent has five parts. Role: who the model is ("You sort customer messages for a small bakery."). Task: the one job. Context: the facts it needs. Rules: what it must and must not do. Output format: exactly how the answer should look.
The system prompt holds the parts that stay the same on every run: role, rules and format. The user message holds what changes each time: the new message to sort, the new question.
Be specific and positive. "Answer in two sentences" works better than "don't be long". Say what to do when unsure: "If the message fits no category, use other." That one rule prevents many wrong guesses.
Step by step:
- Role: who is the model?
- Task: one clear job.
- Context: the facts it needs.
- Rules: must, must not, and what to do when unsure.
- Format: exactly how the answer looks.
Words to know:
- System prompt: the standing instructions sent with every request.
- User message: the part that changes each time, like a new question or input.
Try it now: Write a five-part system prompt for one job in your agent from course 1. Paste it into a free chatbot, then send three different inputs and see if it follows every rule.
You can now write a prompt with a role, task, context, rules and output format.

check.q: What is the role part of a system prompt?
options: The exact JSON keys you want back
The message the user sends this time
The list of test inputs
Who the model should act as, such as a support sorter
check.why: The role tells the model who it is for this job; the other parts cover task, context, rules and format.

check.q: Your prompt says "be helpful and good" and the answers vary. What would you change?
options: Replace it with clear rules the model can follow and you can check
Make the prompt longer with more friendly words
Remove all rules so the model can decide
Switch to a different chatbot
check.why: Vague words cannot be checked; specific rules make behavior consistent.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Examples, steps and structured output
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an example and a JSON format to get answers a program can read.
This lesson builds toward: Given your system prompt, you will add one worked example and an exact JSON output format, so that at least 4 of 5 answers are only valid JSON with the right keys.
Showing beats telling. One or two worked examples in the prompt (input and the exact output you want) improve results a lot. This is called few-shot prompting. Zero-shot means no examples.
Agents need answers that code can read, not chatty paragraphs. Ask for JSON, a simple text format of names and values: {"category": "order", "urgent": false}. Say: "Reply with only JSON, no other text," and show the exact keys.
For harder jobs, ask the model to work in steps: first list the facts, then decide. Many model services can also force valid JSON with a setting called structured output; check your provider's documentation for it.
Words to know:
- Few-shot prompting: giving the model a few examples of input and the right output.
- JSON: a simple text format of named values that programs can read, like {"name": "Ana"}.
- Structured output: a model setting that makes the answer follow an exact format.
Try it now: Add one worked example and a JSON format to your prompt from Lesson 2. Send five inputs. Count how many answers were only JSON with the right keys.
You can now use examples and a JSON format to get answers your code can read.

check.q: Why add a worked example to a prompt?
options: It makes the model run faster
It hides the rules from the user
It shows the model the exact kind of answer you want
It replaces the need for a role
check.why: An example shows the model the pattern and format to copy.

check.q: Some answers come back as JSON with a friendly sentence in front. What would you do?
options: Accept it, because the JSON is in there somewhere
State in the prompt to return only JSON with the exact keys, and show an example
Ask for a longer answer
Remove the output format so the model is free
check.why: Code needs only JSON, so the prompt must say so clearly and show it.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Calling and testing an LLM from Python

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Your first model call from Google Colab
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Call an LLM from a Python notebook and print the answer.
This lesson builds toward: In a free Google Colab notebook, you will call an LLM from Python with the API key stored as a secret, with the answer printed and no key visible in the code.
Google Colab is a free Python notebook that runs in your browser; you need a Google account. Free resources are not guaranteed and idle notebooks time out, so save your work. Open colab.research.google.com and create a new notebook.
To call a model you need an API key, a secret password for programs. Google's Gemini API has a free tier for small projects; you get a key from Google AI Studio (aistudio.google.com/apikey). Google says free-tier content may be used to improve its products, so never send private or customer data on the free tier.
Google's current quickstart shows lines like these: pip install -U google-genai, then from google import genai, client = genai.Client(), then interaction = client.interactions.create(model='MODEL_NAME', input='Explain an AI agent in one sentence'), then print(interaction.output_text). Copy the exact model name and code from the quickstart page, because names and code change. The key is read from an environment variable named GEMINI_API_KEY.
Never paste your key into a shared notebook, a screenshot or a chatbot. Keep it in a secret setting, and make a new key if one leaks. Other providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, or a free local model with Ollama) work the same way: a client, a model name, an input and an output.
Step by step:
- Open colab.research.google.com and make a new notebook.
- Get an API key from Google AI Studio and keep it secret.
- Install the library and copy the quickstart code.
- Use the model name shown on the quickstart page.
- Run the cell and print the answer.
Words to know:
- API: a way for one program to talk to another, like your code asking a model for an answer.
- API key: a secret code that lets your program use a service; treat it like a password.
- Environment variable: a setting stored outside your code, often used for secrets.
Official sources:
- Google Colab FAQ
- Gemini API quickstart
- Gemini API pricing and free tier
Try it now: Make a Colab notebook, set up a key the safe way and get the model to answer: "Explain an AI agent in one sentence." Save the notebook as agent-prompts.
You can now call an LLM from Python in a free notebook and keep your API key secret.

options: A free Python notebook that runs in a web browser
A paid AI model
A place to store passwords
A phone app for chatting with AI
check.why: Colab lets you run Python in the browser for free, with limits.

check.q: You are about to share your notebook. Your API key is typed into a code cell. What do you do?
options: Share it, since only friends will see it
Blur the key in a screenshot instead
Change the variable name so it is harder to find
Move the key into a secret setting, and make a new key if it was already seen
check.why: A key is like a password: keep it in a secret setting and replace it if it leaked.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Sending your system prompt and reading JSON in code
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Send your prompt from code and turn the JSON answer into Python data.
This lesson builds toward: Given a model answer in your notebook, you will parse the JSON answer into Python data and handle a bad answer, without the code crashing on an empty or broken answer.
Put your system prompt in a Python variable: SYSTEM = '''You sort messages for a bakery... Reply with only JSON.''' Put each new input in another variable. The simplest way to combine them is to send SYSTEM plus the input as one text; most providers also have a separate system-instruction setting, shown in their documentation.
Read the answer with Python's json library: import json, then data = json.loads(text). Now data['category'] is a normal Python value your agent can act on.
The model will sometimes add words around the JSON or miss a key. Plan for it: wrap the parse in try and except, and if it fails, either retry once with "Reply with only JSON" or mark the input as failed. Never let a bad answer crash the agent or slip through silently.
Step by step:
- Store the system prompt in a variable.
- Send the system prompt and the input to the model.
- Parse the answer with json.loads inside try / except.
- Check the keys you need are there.
- On failure: retry once, or mark it failed.
Words to know:
- Parse: turn text into data a program can use.
- try / except: Python's way to catch an error and handle it instead of crashing.
- Retry: trying the same request again after a failure.
Try it now: In your notebook, send your system prompt with one input, parse the JSON, and print just the category. Then give it a strange input (an empty message) and make sure your code does not crash.
You can now send a system prompt from Python and safely turn the model's JSON into data.

check.q: What does json.loads do with the model's answer?
options: Sends it back to the model
Turns JSON text into Python data your code can use
Checks whether the answer is true
Saves it to a file
check.why: json.loads parses JSON text into Python data such as a dictionary.

check.q: Your agent gets an empty message and the parse step fails. What should the code do?
options: Crash so you notice it
Return whatever text came back as the category
Catch the error, then retry once or mark the item as failed
Delete the message
check.why: Wrapping the parse in try / except lets the agent handle a bad answer instead of crashing.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Testing a prompt like an engineer
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Run a prompt on a small test set and improve it from the results.
This lesson builds toward: Given five test inputs, including one tricky input, you will test the prompt, record the results and change one thing to fix a failure, rerunning every test after each change.
One good answer proves little. Engineers write a test set: a short list of inputs with the answer they expect. Include easy cases, edge cases (empty, very long, two topics at once) and one tricky case, such as a message that says "ignore your instructions".
In Python, a list of pairs works: tests = [('Where is my cake?', 'order'), ('You burned my bread!', 'complaint')]. Loop over it, call the model, parse the JSON and compare to the expected answer. Count valid JSON and correct answers.
Change one thing at a time: a clearer rule, a better example. Run the whole test set again after each change, so you know the fix helped and broke nothing. Keep each prompt version and its score in your notebook.
Step by step:
- Write 5 to 10 test inputs with expected answers.
- Include edge cases and one tricky input.
- Loop: call, parse, compare, count.
- Change one thing in the prompt.
- Run all tests again and keep the better version.
Words to know:
- Test set: a list of inputs with the answers you expect, used to check a prompt.
- Edge case: an unusual input, like an empty or very long message.
- Regression: when a change fixes one thing but breaks another.
Try it now: Final task: write your system prompt with role, task, three rules, a JSON format and one example. Test it in Colab on five inputs including one tricky one, record valid JSON and correct for each, change the prompt once to fix a failure, and rerun.
You can now test and improve a prompt with a small test set, the way agent builders do.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Complete system prompt One or more of role, task or three rules is missing or vague. Gives a role, the task and three clear rules. Rules also cover what to do when unsure or when nothing fits. Format and example No exact JSON format or no example. States the exact JSON keys and gives one worked example. The example matches the format exactly and most outputs are valid JSON. Runs from Colab safely The notebook does not run, or the API key is visible. The prompt runs from Colab with the key kept in a secret setting. The notebook is tidy and someone else could rerun it with their own key. Parses answers safely A bad or empty answer crashes the code. JSON is parsed into data and a bad answer is caught. Failed items are marked clearly so they can be reviewed. Tested and improved Fewer than five inputs, no tricky input, or results not recorded. Five inputs including one tricky one, valid JSON and correct recorded for each, one change made and all tests rerun. Can explain why the failure happened and what the change fixed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a regression when you test prompts?
options: A test that passes the first time
A fix that makes a test that used to pass now fail
A test input written in another language
A slower answer from the model
check.why: A regression is when a change breaks something that worked before.

check.q: One of five tests fails. What is the best next step?
options: Change one thing in the prompt and rerun all five tests
Rewrite the whole prompt from the start
Delete the failing test
Rerun only the failing test
check.why: Changing one thing and rerunning every test shows what the change fixed and what it broke.
